title: Modern physics: relativity, quanta, atoms, nuclei
note: Special relativity starts from two postulates: physics is the same in every inertial frame, and light's speed is c for all observers. Quantum physics adds that light and matter come in discrete packets: photons carry E = hf, atoms have discrete energy levels, and unstable nuclei decay with a fixed half-life.

read.title: Where classical physics ends
text: By 1900 physics seemed nearly complete, yet two puzzles broke it open. The first was light's speed. Einstein took the experimental result seriously: every observer measures the same c, whatever their motion. Combined with the rule that physics works the same in every inertial frame, this forces time and space to adjust. Moving clocks run slow, moving objects are shorter along their motion, and mass and energy become interchangeable through E = mc². None of this is noticeable at everyday speeds, but GPS satellites must correct for relativity to stay accurate.

The second puzzle concerned light and matter at small scales. In the photoelectric effect, light ejects electrons from a metal, but only if its frequency is high enough; making dim red light brighter never works. Einstein explained this with photons, packets of energy hf. Atoms likewise absorb and emit only specific energies, because electrons occupy discrete levels, which is why each element has its own spectral fingerprint. Particles even have wavelengths, λ = h/p.

Deeper still, the nucleus holds protons and neutrons together with the strong force. Unstable nuclei decay at random, yet a large sample loses half its nuclei every half-life. Splitting heavy nuclei or fusing light ones releases energy, because the products are more tightly bound.

q.q: Why does brighter red light fail to eject electrons in the photoelectric effect?
o: Each photon's energy depends on frequency, not brightness

q.q: Why does each element have its own spectrum?
o: Its electrons occupy discrete energy levels
Its atoms move at different speeds

q.q: Why do fission and fusion both release energy?
o: The products are more tightly bound
